# Status report: jf2 allocator test on kestrel, 2026-11-20

## Short version

We tested jf2 (our fork of the jemalloc memory allocator) in kestrel (our key-value store). At near-equal throughput, the p99 latency (99% of requests are faster) fell from 2140 us to 870 us. The capacity team must still approve the cost of 5.7 GB (9.3%) more memory.

## Words used here

- **jemalloc 5.3**: the open-source memory allocator that kestrel uses today.
- **Build A**: commit main@4f1c2aa with jemalloc 5.3.
- **Build B**: the same commit with jf2.
- **ycsb-b**: the read-heavy workload of YCSB (Yahoo Cloud Serving Benchmark).
- **ycsb-a**: the write-heavy workload of the same benchmark.
- **p50, p99.9**: the same measure as p99, for 50% and 99.9% of requests.
- **kops/s**: thousand operations per second.
- **us**: microseconds.
- **RSS** (resident set size): the physical memory that the process holds.
- **Decay purge**: jemalloc returns unused memory to the operating system after a delay.
- **perf**: the Linux profiling tool.
- **je_arena_decay**: the jemalloc function that runs the decay purge.
- **logrotate**: a system tool that archives log files.
- **NUMA pinning**: binding the process to the processors and memory of one socket. NUMA means non-uniform memory access.
- **Feature flag**: a configuration switch that turns a change on or off.
- **Staging**: the pre-production environment.
- **bench-07**: the test host.

## Test setup

- **Host**: bench-07 has 2 Xeon processors with 32 cores each and 512 GB of memory. It runs Linux kernel 6.8.
- **System load before the runs**: the load average was 0.4 (near idle for 64 cores).
- **Builds**: build A and build B differ only in the allocator.
- **Workload**: ycsb-b with 64 client threads.
- **Runs**: 5 runs per build, 10 minutes per run. The runs alternated between the builds (A, B, A, B, and so on).

## Results

Latency of the slow requests, in us. Lower is better.

```
us      0        2000      4000      6000      8000     10000
        |---------|---------|---------|---------|---------|
p99         B======A  -1270 us (-59.3%)
           870    2140
p99.9                   B================================A
                       3100     -6700 us (-68.4%)      9800

A = build A (jemalloc 5.3)    B = build B (jf2)
```

Each dot is the median of 5 runs. One column is 200 us.

**Takeaway**: only the slow-request latencies moved. Throughput and median latency stayed inside their ranges.

Each cell shows the median of 5 runs, then the range (lowest to highest run).

| Metric | Build A (jemalloc 5.3) | Build B (jf2) | Change | Ranges overlap? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Throughput, kops/s | 412 (405 to 418) | 409 (401 to 415) | -3 (-0.7%) | Yes |
| p50 latency, us | 118 (116 to 121) | 119 (117 to 121) | +1 (+0.8%) | Yes |
| p99 latency, us | 2140 (1890 to 2610) | 870 (820 to 940) | -1270 (-59.3%) | No |
| p99.9 latency, us | 9800 (7200 to 14100) | 3100 (2700 to 3900) | -6700 (-68.4%) | No |
| RSS at end, GB | 61.2 | 66.9 | +5.7 (+9.3%) | Range not reported |

What the data shows:

- **p99 latency**: build B is 1270 us (59.3%) lower. The ranges of the two builds do not overlap [Ref1].
- **p99.9 latency**: build B is 6700 us (68.4%) lower. The ranges do not overlap [Ref1].
- **Throughput**: build B is 3 kops/s (0.7%) lower. The ranges overlap. So this test does not show a throughput difference [Ref1].
- **p50 latency**: build B is 1 us (0.8%) higher. The ranges overlap. So this test does not show a median-latency difference [Ref1].
- **Stability between runs**: the p99 range is 720 us wide for build A. It is 120 us wide for build B [Ref1].
- **RSS**: build B ends 5.7 GB (9.3%) higher [Ref1].

## Cause of the spikes

- **Observation**: the spikes in build A occur at the same time as the decay purge [Ref2].
- **Profile data**: perf attributes 31% of the samples taken during spikes to je_arena_decay [Ref2].
- **Difference in build B**: jf2 runs the purge in a background thread.
- **Hypothesis**: the background thread is the reason for the lower p99 and p99.9. A perf profile of build B under the same workload would confirm or reject this.

## One run was replaced

1. Run 3 of build B stalled for 40 s at minute 7.
2. We traced the stall to logrotate [Ref3]. A nightly scheduled job started it.
3. The allocator did not cause the stall [Ref3].
4. We reran run 3. The build B figures use the rerun in place of the stalled run.

## Not tested

**Insufficient data** for the three cases below. A run of each case would resolve it.

- ycsb-a (planned for tomorrow)
- more than 64 client threads
- NUMA pinning

## Open question

- Is 5.7 GB (9.3%) more RSS acceptable? The capacity team must answer this.

## Next steps

1. Run ycsb-a tomorrow (2026-11-21).
2. Ask the capacity team to approve the RSS increase.
3. If the capacity team approves, enable jf2 in staging, controlled by a feature flag.

## References

- [Ref1] Runs of 2026-11-20 on bench-07: ycsb-b, 5 runs per build, median and range.
- [Ref2] perf profile of build A from the same runs, sampled during the latency spikes.
- [Ref3] Investigation of the 40 s stall in run 3 of build B.

---

Three points I could not settle from your notes:

- **RSS range**: the notes give one RSS value per build. The table marks the range as "not reported".
- **"if ok"**: I read it as approval from the capacity team only. Add the ycsb-a result to step 3 if it is also a condition.
- **Cause**: the notes hold no profile of build B. So the report labels the cause as a hypothesis.
